g.text: NT Lan Manager (NTLM/MS-NLMP), a family of security protocols
--> consisting of LM, NTLMv1, and NTLMv2
--> used by application protocols on various Windows-based networks to authenticate remote users and
optionally provide session security when requested by the application.
--> NTLM security protocols are all "embedded protocols", it does not have a network protocol stack layer, allowing
any protocol with a defined layer in the network stack (such as SMB, HTTP(S), and LDAP(S)) to utilize it.
For the application protocol using it, NTLMv2 provides three primary operations:
• Message integrity, known as message "signing" in the NTLM terminology.
• Message confidentiality, known as message "sealing" in the NTLM terminology.
--> NTLM is a challenge-response protocol that uses nonces as a defensive mechanism against replaying attacks.
--> NTLM is best implemented as a function library that can be called by application protocols rather than as a layer
--> Both domain-joined and workgroup computers can utilize NTLM for authentication;
• The NTLM version used on hosts, whether NTLMv1 or NTLMv2, is configured out-of-band* before authentication.
• Using a secure mechanism, the client and server/DC share a secret key (the user's password's hash) before
• Neither plaintext credentials nor the shared secret key are sent over the wire.
is an API that allows connected applications to call one of several security providers to establish authenticated
connections and to exchange data securely over those connections.
A "security support provider" (SSP) is a dynamic-link library (DLL) responsible for implementing the SSPI by
exposing one or more security packages to applications; each security package provides mappings between an
application's SSPI function calls and an actual security model's functions. These security packages support various
NTLM SSP (located at %Windir%\System32\msv1_0.dll) is a binary messaging protocol utilized by SSPI to
facilitate NTLM challenge-response authentication and to negotiate options for integrity and confidentiality. The
NTLM SSP encompasses both the NTLM and NTLMv2 authentication protocols. .
out-of-band : separately from the authentication process itself. This means that the choice of NTLM version is determined in advance, typically through system
policies, registry settings, or Group Policy configurations on the hosts, rather than being negotiated dynamically during authentication.

NTLMv1, which has been replaced by NTLMv2, only supports signing (ensuring data integrity) but
not sealing (encryption for confidentiality). NTLMv2 improves security by adding support for both
signing and sealing, making it more resistant to attacks like replay and man-in-the-middle.
In the context of NTLM, sealing also implies signing because every sealed message is also signed.

If the client and server negotiate it, session security provides message
The NTLM protocol itself does not provide session security; instead, SSPI
NTLMv1, supplanted by NTLMv2, does not support sealing but only signing;
therefore, Microsoft strongly recommends against its usage (and the
Message signing provides message integrity and helps
--> When session signing is negotiated, the client and
server negotiate a session key to sign all messages
--> The session key is generated using a combination of
the client's and server's challenge messages and the
--> Once the session key is established, all messages
between the client and server are signed using a MAC.
--> The MAC is generated by applying a cryptographic
algorithm to the message and the session key. The
server can verify the MAC by using the same algorithm
as the message and the session key and comparing the
result to the MAC provided by the client.
Although an adversary might be eavesdropping, they
don't possess the user's password hash since it is never
transmitted over the wire, and therefore cannot sign
We can know the default SMB signing settings for hosts
in the network depending on the SMB version they are
running. Except for SMB1, which has three possible
settings, Required, Enabled, or Disabled, SMB2 and
SMB3 only have Required or Not Required:
Message sealing provides message confidentiality by
implementing a symmetric-key encryption mechanism; it
ensures that the content of the messages exchanged
between the client and server remains secure and that
adversaries cannot read or tamper with them.
Similar to the Oracle Session attack, NTLM relay (also referred to as "NTLM
reflection") is an infamous Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) (also known as Man-in-the-
Middle (MitM) or Bucket Brigade Attack) technique abused by many vulnerabilities and
attacks to gain unauthorized access to resources on a network.
Regardless of the many security improvements that NTLMv2 received over NTLMv1 and
LM, all of the NTLM family of authentication protocols are susceptible to relay
attacks from spoofed servers because they lack the means of supporting mutual
--> the session security SSPI provides tackles this problem using signing.
--> Against domain-joined machines, an adversary pretends to be a legitimate server for
the client requesting authentication, in addition to pretending to be a legitimate client for
the server that offers a service, relaying messages back and forth between them until
--> After establishing an authenticated session with the server, the adversary abuses it
to carry out authorized actions on behalf of the client;
--> for the client, the adversary either sends an application message stating that
authentication failed or terminates the connection:

The pre-relay phase focuses on techniques that
induce/coerce a client to initiate NTLM authentication
for a service on a server:
Many techniques are used in the pre-relay phase, including:
• AiTM techniques such as poisoning and spoofing attacks.
These techniques usually make much noise and are opportunistic
because many rely on requests and traffic initiated by the clients.
Windows supports various name resolution processes:
While DNS is a unicast protocol, meaning that a client
directly asks a server for a name resolution, the LLMNR,
NBT-NS, and mDNS are multicast protocols, meaning that
the client will broadcast the network asking if anyone
knows the name it's looking for. So, if we are in that
network, we can answer random name resolution requests
and redirect the client to our attack host.

The post-relay phase takes advantage of the authenticated session we obtained
through relaying a victim's NTLM authentication. We can conduct specific post-relay
attacks depending on the authenticated session's protocol.

- DCE RPC (C706) defines remote procedure call mechanisms for executing functions on remote systems.
- MS-RPCE extends C706, adding security features and authentication methods like NTLM, Kerberos, and TLS.
- Some RPC interfaces accept RPC_C_AUTHN_LEVEL_CONNECT, making them vulnerable to NTLM relay attacks.
- MS-TSCH (Task Scheduler Service) → Can relay NTLM for remote command execution.
- MS-ICPR (ICertPassage for AD CS) → Enables cross-protocol relay attacks (ESC11).
- ntlmrelayx can relay NTLM authentication over TSCH for RCE on Microsoft Exchange Servers.
- Advanced attacks target AD CS, using ICPR to escalate privileges via ESC11.
- Identify RPC interfaces that allow NTLM relay.
- Exploit weak authentication levels (e.g., CONNECT) to hijack NTLM sessions.
- Target Exchange Servers and AD CS for post-relay attacks.

• PORT specifies an arbitrary port the WebDAV service will use to connect to the attack machine.
• PATH specifies an arbitrary path the WebDAV service will attempt to connect.
PrinterBug exploits the Print Spooler Service via the MS-RPRN protocol to coerce SMB NTLM authentication. It abuses
the RpcRemoteFindFirstPrinterChangeNotificationEx method to force a domain-joined machine to authenticate to an
attacker-controlled system. Tools like printerbug.py, MSRPRN-coerce, and SpoolSample automate this attack.
printerbug.py can be used with ntlmrelayx to relay authentication for privilege escalation or lateral movement.
PetitPotam exploits MS-EFSR (Encrypting File System Remote Protocol) to coerce SMB NTLM authentication by
abusing EfsRpcOpenFileRaw and EfsRpcEncryptFileSrv. Before CVE-2021-36942, attackers could exploit this without
valid domain credentials. If patched, alternative implementations like ly4k's PetitPotam may still work. Tools like
PetitPotam.py can relay authentication via ntlmrelayx for privilege escalation or lateral movement.
try ly4k's PetitPotam if the original doesn't work

RBCD allows a computer to authenticate on behalf of others by modifying its **msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity** attribute. Attackers can abuse this via
**NTLM relay** by coercing a machine to authenticate and relaying it over **LDAP** to the DC, granting control over a target machine. This requires **WebClient (WebDAV)
enabled** or bypassing session signing using **CVE-2019-1040** with `ntlmrelayx --remove-mic`. RBCD can be used for **privilege escalation and lateral movement** in Active

Advanced NTLM Relay Attacks Targeting AD CS
**NTLM Cross-Protocol Relay Attacks on AD CS (ESC8 & ESC11):**
Attackers can **relay NTLM authentication over HTTP** to exploit **Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS)** and obtain certificates for
privilege escalation. By targeting **HTTP-based enrollment endpoints** (`certsrv/certfnsh.asp`), attackers can request certificates using relayed
NTLM sessions. Tools like **CrackMapExec (adcs module)** help identify AD CS instances. Under **ESC8 and ESC11**, this enables impersonation
of authenticated users, facilitating lateral movement and domain persistence.
